context.title: Coder Agents choose where code runs, but developers can't easily see or steer that choice
context.body: With Coder Agents, a developer describes the work and the agent picks a template, provisions a workspace and gets going. The template decides the network the agent can reach and the resources it uses, and the agent chooses it from template descriptions. Once it's working, follow-up messages wait until the current step finishes. Both are sensible defaults, but they're invisible at the moment a developer would want to step in: before the workspace starts, and while a long step runs.
assumptions: I haven't used Coder Agents. My view comes from Coder's docs (v2.39), so the UI may already differ.
The docs say users can choose a workspace when starting a chat; they don't say whether the agent's automatic choice is shown or can be changed. The concept assumes it isn't, prominently.
The 10-second start window and 'Deliver now' are proposals; interrupting may need agent-side support.
Visual language approximates Coder's dark dashboard (zinc greys, sky-blue accent, Inter and a mono face). No Coder logo.
The repo, templates and people are fictional.

goals.title: See where the agent will work
goals.body: Show the template it picked, why, and its network and size, before it starts.

goals.title: Change it cheaply
goals.body: Switch template, or reuse a running workspace, in one click.

goals.title: Steer without guessing
goals.body: Show when a queued message will land, and offer to deliver it now.

jtbd: When I hand a task to an agent, I want to know where it will run and be able to redirect it mid-task, so I trust it with real repos without watching every step.

evidence.finding: Developers describe the work and Coder Agents handles 'selecting a template, provisioning a workspace, and executing the task', routing on template descriptions.
Agent workspaces have the same network access as manual ones unless the template restricts it; Coder recommends dedicated agent templates with stricter network policies.
The docs say users 'can also manually choose which workspace is used when starting a new chat', and suggest reviewing template descriptions if the agent picks the wrong one.
'Messages are queued and delivered when the agent completes its current step'; interrupting is documented for sub-agents.

evidence.step: The role is about human–AI collaboration
evidence.finding: The designer will 'define how humans and AI collaborate in developer tooling', end to end with PMs and engineers.

approaches: Name the chosen template in the chat
Show why it was chosen, with network and size
Give a short window to switch or reuse a workspace
Show queued messages and when they'll be delivered
Offer 'Deliver now' with the cost of interrupting
End with a review card: diff, tests, workspace lifetime

ranges.title: Name the template
ranges.summary: A line in the chat saying which template the agent picked.

ranges.title: Show the queue
ranges.summary: Queued follow-ups shown with when they'll be delivered.

screens.alt: Sketch: queued message with delivery time

ranges.title: Workspace Check
ranges.summary: A workspace card with the reason, network and size and a window to switch, queued messages with 'Deliver now', and a review card when the work is ready.
pros: Puts the developer in control at the two moments that matter.
Makes governance (network policy) visible, not just enforced.
cons: A start window adds a few seconds.

screens.alt: Sketch: queued message with Deliver now
screens.label: Steer

decision.title: Workspace Check: see and steer where the agent works
decision.body: Range 3. Before provisioning, a card shows the template the agent chose, why, and its network and size, with 10 seconds to switch or reuse a running workspace. While it works, queued messages show when they'll land, with 'Deliver now'. At the end, a review card shows the diff, tests and when the workspace stops.
reasons: The template decides what the agent can reach, so it deserves a glance.
Steering is how developers build trust in agents; hiding the queue makes them repeat themselves.
It makes platform teams' routing visible to developers, so bad descriptions get fixed.
decision.tradeoff: The start window slows every run a little. I'd make it skippable per template and measure how often people switch.

depth.body: Built in a Coder-like dark dashboard. Three moments in a chat about a refund rounding bug: the agent's workspace card (python-payments, chosen because its description matches, Payments VPC only) with a 10-second window and alternatives including a running workspace; a queued follow-up that says it'll land after the test suite, with 'Deliver now'; and a review card with the diff, passing tests, a draft PR and when the workspace stops. Cards ease in, and motion turns off for people who reduce it.

validation.method: I'd look at how often agent chats are restarted after the workspace starts, and how often developers repeat a message, then test the card with platform teams and developers.
hypotheses: Developers switch template in a small but meaningful share of runs, mostly when descriptions are vague.
Fewer duplicate follow-up messages when the queue is visible.
Fewer chats restarted because of the wrong workspace.

metrics.name: Template switch rate
metrics.definition: Share of agent runs where the developer changes the template in the start window.

metrics.name: Duplicate follow-ups
metrics.definition: Follow-up messages repeated within 5 minutes, per chat.

metrics.name: Restarted chats
metrics.definition: Chats abandoned and restarted within 10 minutes of provisioning.

nextSteps: Check with engineering what the agent knows when it picks a template.
Review template descriptions with two platform teams.
Test the card and queue with five developers on real repos.
Explore the same pattern for sub-agents.
